title: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
summary: How SPLADE turns BERT's MLM logits into sparse expanded term weights, trains them with FLOPs and distillation, makes queries fast, and runs on SciFact.
outcomes: Explain why vocabulary mismatch hurts BM25 and how learned expansion keeps an inverted index
Compute SPLADE term weights w_j = max_i log(1 + ReLU(w_ij)) from a small logit matrix
Compute a sparse dot-product score by traversing posting lists, in bi-encoder and doc-only modes
Explain why the FLOPs regularizer balances posting lists better than L1
Compute MarginMSE and KL distillation losses and the direction they move term weights
Explain why SPLADE queries defeat MaxScore and WAND, and trace Block-Max Pruning
Encode, index and evaluate a SPLADE model on a BEIR dataset against BM25
Choose SPLADE settings (lambda, doc-only mode, pruning, chunking) for a production engine

lessons.title: Why learn sparse vectors instead of dense ones

blocks.md: BM25 scores a document only on the query words it literally contains, weighted by rarity and saturated by term frequency, and it runs fast because an **inverted index** maps each term to the short list of documents that contain it. Its weakness is **vocabulary mismatch**: a relevant document that says *car* gets nothing for a query that says *auto*.

Dense retrieval fixes mismatch by embedding text into a few hundred dimensions, but every dimension is non-zero, so it needs an approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) index such as an HNSW graph instead of an inverted index, and it loses exact term matching. It also loses the reason for a match. Give D1 and the query below an illustrative 4-dimensional embedding: D1 about (0.61, -0.22, 0.48, 0.59), the query about (0.52, -0.35, 0.41, 0.67). Their cosine is 0.98, mostly from dimensions 4 (0.39) and 1 (0.32), but no dimension has a name, so nothing says *why* they match.

**Learned sparse retrieval** keeps the BM25 machinery and changes only where the weights come from: a transformer writes a weight for every term of the vocabulary, almost all of them zero. The non-zeros can include terms the text never used. That is **expansion**, and every match can be read off by term, as the figure below shows.

We use one running example in the whole course. The vocabulary has 10 terms (real SPLADE uses the 30,522 WordPiece tokens of BERT). BERT, short for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers, is the pre-trained transformer encoder SPLADE starts from, and WordPiece is its tokenizer: common words are single tokens and rarer words are split into frequent pieces, so a fixed list of 30,522 entries covers any English text. The document **D1** is *fix my car engine*; the query is *auto repair*. A human would call D1 relevant, yet they share no word.

blocks.title: Bag of words versus a learned sparse vector

scenes.caption: As a bag of words, D1 has 1s on fix, my, car, engine and the query has 1s on auto and repair. No column is non-zero in both, so the dot product, and the BM25 score, is exactly 0.
SPLADE replaces the 1s with learned weights for D1. Weights appear on auto, motor, repair and price, words D1 never contains: these are expansion terms (orange).
The query is encoded the same way. It keeps auto and repair and adds car, engine, motor and fix. The query now has 6 non-zeros instead of 2.
Six columns are now non-zero on both sides (green). The score is the dot product over those columns: 6.60 instead of 0. my and price stay in D1 but cost nothing here because the query weight is 0.

blocks.md: A learned sparse vector is still a bag of weighted terms, so it can live in a normal inverted index. The transformer only decides *which* terms get *how much* weight, including terms absent from the text.

SPLADE (SParse Lexical AnD Expansion model, Formal, Piwowarski and Clinchant, SIGIR 2021) is the best known model of this kind. SIGIR, named after the ACM Special Interest Group on Information Retrieval that runs it, is the main research conference on information retrieval. It was not the first: DeepCT learned weights only for terms already in the text, doc2query used a text generation model to predict queries a document could answer and appended them to the document, and SparTerm predicted weights over the whole vocabulary but needed a separately trained gate, a second component that decides which vocabulary terms to switch on. SPLADE made the sparse representation trainable end to end with a log saturation and an explicit sparsity regularizer, the two ideas this course builds up.

blocks.question: Query: auto repair. Document: fix my car engine. Why does BM25 give this document a score of exactly 0, no matter how k1 and b are tuned?
options: Because the document is too short for length normalization
Because the IDF of auto is negative
Because BM25 needs at least two matching terms
Because BM25 only sums over query terms present in the document, and none are
blocks.explain: BM25 is a sum over query terms that occur in the document. With zero overlapping terms the sum is empty, so tuning cannot help. Expansion is what creates overlap.

blocks.question: What does learned sparse retrieval keep from BM25, and what does it replace?
options: Keeps the inverted index and dot-product style scoring, replaces hand-made term weights with learned ones that may include new terms
Keeps the dense embedding, replaces the ANN index
Keeps the BM25 formula, replaces the tokenizer
Keeps nothing; it is a re-ranker
blocks.explain: The index structure and term-at-a-time scoring (walking one query term's posting list at a time and adding up scores, lesson 3) stay. The weights now come from a transformer and can sit on vocabulary terms the text never used.

lessons.title: From MLM logits to one weight per vocabulary term

blocks.md: BERT is a transformer encoder (as in the transformer course) pre-trained as a masked language model (MLM): about 15% of the input tokens are picked, most of them replaced by a special mask token, and the model learns to predict the original words from the context on both sides. It turns each input token into a contextual vector $h_i$, and its MLM head (a small output layer on top of the encoder) scores every vocabulary entry as a possible word at that position. SPLADE reuses exactly that head. For input token $i$ and vocabulary term $j$ it computes a **logit** $w_{ij}$, a raw score that can be any real number, positive or negative. A softmax over a row would turn these scores into probabilities, but SPLADE never applies one; it uses the raw logits, one for each of the $|V|$ vocabulary terms:

blocks.caption: In words: the dot product of the transformed token with the input embedding $E_j$ of term $j$, plus a bias $b_j$: high when term $j$ fits that position. transform is a linear layer, GeLU, then LayerNorm (both explained next). It is the MLM prediction, so it starts from a pre-trained MLM checkpoint.

blocks.md: GeLU (Gaussian error linear unit) multiplies its input $x$ by the probability that a standard Gaussian variable is below $x$; that probability is computed with the Gauss error function, which is where the name comes from. The result is a smooth version of ReLU (rectified linear unit), which is $\max(0, x)$: large positive inputs pass almost unchanged and large negative ones go to almost 0. LayerNorm, as in the transformer course, rescales each vector to zero mean and unit variance.

That gives a matrix with one row per input token and one column per vocabulary term (here 4 x 10; for real BERT, N x 30,522, where N is the number of input tokens). SPLADE v2 turns the matrix into one vector with two steps: **ReLU then log** on every cell, then **max pooling** down each column. As defined above, ReLU sets every negative logit to 0 and keeps positive ones. Max pooling keeps only the largest value in each column.

blocks.caption: For each vocabulary term $j$, take log(1 + ReLU) of its logit at every position $i$ of the input text $t$ and keep the largest. The natural log. The original SPLADE (2021) summed over $i$; SPLADE v2 switched to max.

blocks.title: Logits for fix my car engine (illustrative values)

scenes.caption: Raw MLM logits (made-up but plausible numbers for this toy). The car row is high on car and auto; the fix row is high on fix and repair; the engine row is high on engine and motor. Most cells are negative.
ReLU sets every negative logit to 0. Already 24 of the 40 cells are exactly zero, including the whole banana and bread columns.
log(1 + x) compresses what is left: 3.5 becomes 1.50 and 3.2 becomes 1.44, while small values barely change (0.3 becomes 0.26). Large logits can no longer dominate.

Max pooling keeps the largest cell in each column (highlighted). auto comes from the car row, repair from the fix row, motor from the engine row: each expansion term is traced to the token that produced it.

blocks.title: The pooled document vector

scenes.caption: Max pooling gives D1 eight non-zero weights out of ten. engine (1.50), car (1.44) and fix (1.39) are the strongest; my gets a small 0.47.
Sum pooling (original SPLADE) adds every row instead: car becomes 2.31 because fix, car and engine all vote for it. Terms that many tokens mildly support get inflated.

blocks.title: Why the log: saturation of a single logit

scenes.caption: Without the log, a logit of 8 would weigh 8 times a logit of 1. With it, the ratio is 2.20 / 0.69 = 3.2. The paper links this to the log of term frequency (tf) used to saturate counts in classic IR.
Negative logits stay at exactly 0 on both curves. That exact zero, not a small number, is what keeps the term out of the inverted index.

blocks.prompt: The SparTerm baseline used ReLU without the log and needed a separate gating step for sparsity. With nothing else changed, what do you expect adding log(1 + .) did to the number of non-zero weights?
blocks.reveal: It made the vectors much **sparser**. The SPLADE paper reports this was surprising: the log saturation alone already gave sparse solutions without any regularization, and with expansion plus a sparsity loss SPLADE cut the estimated FLOPs from 4.62 (SparTerm-style expansion, no log) to 0.88 at similar quality. This cost is the average number of multiplications needed to score one query against one document on the inverted index (lesson 4 derives it).

blocks.md: Why did max pooling help? First, how quality is measured. MS MARCO (Microsoft Machine Reading Comprehension) is the standard training and test collection for passage ranking: about 8.8 million passages from web pages and over 500,000 real Bing search queries for training, each usually with one passage marked relevant. Results are reported on its dev set (development set) of 6,980 queries. MRR@10 averages, over queries, 1 divided by the rank of the first relevant passage in the top 10 (0 if none), so a first relevant passage at rank 2 counts one half. The SPLADE v2 paper reports almost 2 points of MRR@10 on MS MARCO (0.322 to 0.340) from that single change.

ColBERT is a retriever that keeps one vector per token and scores a query by matching each query token to its most similar document token and summing those best matches; that is called late interaction, because query and document meet only at scoring time. With max, each vocabulary term is scored by its single strongest supporter, much like a ColBERT-style late interaction picks the best match per query token, rather than accumulating weak evidence from every token.

Misconception: the expansion terms are synonyms. They are whatever the MLM head plus ranking training found useful. The paper's own example document about bow legs gains *leg* and *treatment*, but also *arrow* (bow and arrow) and *teeth*, with small weights.

blocks.code:
out = mlm(**tokens).logits                      # (batch, seq_len, 30522)
acts = torch.log(1 + torch.relu(out))
acts = acts * tokens["attention_mask"].unsqueeze(-1)  # padding gives 0
rep, _ = torch.max(acts, dim=1)                   # (batch, 30522), mostly zeros
blocks.caption: Same computation as the encode method of the Splade class in naver/splade, the official SPLADE code that Naver released on GitHub (agg=max). Masking with 0 is safe under max because all activations are non-negative.

blocks.question: A token's logit for vocabulary term j is -0.7 at every position of the input. What is $w_j$?
options: Exactly 0, so term j is absent from the index entry of this text
A small positive number from the bias b_j
blocks.explain: ReLU maps -0.7 to 0, log(1 + 0) = 0, and the max over positions of zeros is 0. Exact zeros are what make the vector sparse.

blocks.question: Using the matrix above, which input token produced D1's weight for repair, and what is that weight?
options: engine, 0.64
car, 0
repair itself, 1.16
blocks.explain: The fix row has logit 2.2 on repair; log(1 + 2.2) = 1.16 beats engine's log(1 + 0.9) = 0.64. repair is not an input token at all; it is an expansion term.

lessons.title: Scoring as a sparse dot product over an inverted index

blocks.md: The relevance score is a plain dot product between the query vector and the document vector. Because both are mostly zeros, only terms non-zero on *both* sides contribute:

blocks.caption: In words: multiply the query weight and the document weight of each vocabulary term and add the products. The second form is the same sum with the zero products left out.

blocks.md:
Add three more documents to the toy collection. Their vectors are given (assume the same encoder produced them):

- **D2** *used car price*: car 1.90, auto 0.80, price 2.10
- **D3** *banana bread*: banana 2.40, bread 2.20
- **D4** *engine repair cost*: engine 1.60, repair 2.00, motor 0.70, fix 0.90, price 0.60

The query *auto repair* encodes to car 0.83, auto 1.39, engine 0.47, motor 0.34, fix 0.96, repair 1.28.

blocks.prompt: BM25 on the raw text would match only D4, the one document containing repair. Before stepping through the index, which document do you expect SPLADE to rank first, and will D3 be scored at all?
blocks.reveal: D1 wins with 6.60, because six of its terms overlap the expanded query, and every one of those six matches exists only through expansion (on the query side, the document side or both), since the raw texts share no word. D4 is second at 4.41 and D2 third at 2.69. D3 is never scored: none of its postings lie on a query term's list.

blocks.md: The index computes this sum **term-at-a-time**: it walks one query term's posting list at a time and adds query weight times document weight into an **accumulator**, a running score per document. Engines can also go **document-at-a-time**, moving through all the query terms' lists together in document order and finishing one document's score before the next; both read the same postings.

blocks.title: Term-at-a-time scoring of auto repair

scenes.caption: Offline, every document vector is inverted: each term with a non-zero weight gets a posting (doc, weight). Our 4 documents produce 18 postings over 10 terms.
Query term car (weight 0.83) walks its posting list. D1 gets 0.83 x 1.44 = 1.20 and D2 gets 0.83 x 1.90 = 1.58.
Query term auto (weight 1.39) walks its posting list. auto is a literal query word, but an expansion term in both D1 and D2. D1 now 2.72, D2 2.69.
Query term engine (weight 0.47) walks its posting list. D4 enters the accumulator for the first time.
Query term motor (weight 0.34) walks its posting list. motor never appears in any text, only in expansions, yet it still adds 0.35 to D1.
Query term fix (weight 0.96) walks its posting list. D1 reaches 5.11.
Query term repair (weight 1.28) walks its posting list. repair is the only query word that literally occurs in a document text (D4). D4 gets 1.28 x 2.00 = 2.56.
Done: D1 6.60, D4 4.41, D2 2.69. D3 (banana bread) was never touched. Only 12 postings were read, not 4 x 10 products.

blocks.md: Cost is driven by the total length of the posting lists the query touches, not by vocabulary size. Every extra query expansion term and every long posting list is extra work. That is why sparsity, especially on the query side, is the thing training must control.

Real engines store integer **impacts**, not floats: an impact is a term's precomputed score contribution for one document, stored in its posting. The naver/splade repo exports to Anserini (a research toolkit built on Lucene, the open-source search library under Elasticsearch and OpenSearch) with a quantization factor (for example 100, so 1.44 is stored as 144), and DeepImpact (a learned sparse model from lesson 7) quantized its impacts to 8 bits with no loss it could measure. The same dynamic pruning algorithms apply, such as MaxScore and WAND (weak AND): each keeps, for every query term, an upper bound on what it can add (its query weight times the largest weight in its posting list), and skips a document when the bounds of the terms it can still match add up to less than the current k-th best score. On SPLADE they skip far less than on BM25, because expanded queries are long and the weights are flat; lesson 6 shows why and what works instead.

There is a cheaper variant. **SPLADE-doc** (SPLADE v2 paper) has no query encoder: the query is just its tokens, each with weight 1, so the score is the sum of the document's weights on the query's tokens, $s(q,d) = \sum_{j \in q} w^{\text{d}}_j$. All neural work happens at indexing time. OpenSearch, the open-source search engine forked from Elasticsearch, calls this *doc-only mode* (its default) and the full model *bi-encoder mode*, because query and document each go through the encoder on their own.

blocks.title: Toy scores: full SPLADE versus doc-only

scenes.caption: Full SPLADE (query expanded to 6 terms, 12 postings read): D1 6.60, D4 4.41, D2 2.69, D3 0.

Doc-only with the same document vectors: the query is just auto and repair with weight 1, so only 4 postings are read. D1 2.26, D4 2.00, D2 0.80. The order survives here because D1's own expansion already added auto and repair.

blocks.question: A query expands to 40 non-zero terms, many of them common words with long posting lists. What happens to latency compared to a 6-term expansion?
options: Nothing; the dot product is computed on the GPU in constant time
It grows roughly with the total length of the touched posting lists, so it can get much slower
It shrinks, because more terms let WAND prune earlier
It depends only on the number of documents in the collection
blocks.explain: Term-at-a-time or document-at-a-time traversal reads every posting on every query term's list (minus what pruning skips). More and longer lists mean more work, which is why query sparsity is penalized harder.

blocks.question: In doc-only mode, what work remains at query time?
options: Tokenizing the query and traversing the inverted index
Running the full transformer on the query
Re-encoding every candidate document
Nothing; results are precomputed per query
blocks.explain: The query is tokenized with the same vocabulary and each token gets a fixed weight (1 in SPLADE-doc, or a lookup table in OpenSearch). No transformer runs at query time.

lessons.title: Training: ranking loss plus the FLOPs regularizer

blocks.md: SPLADE is trained on MS MARCO with a contrastive ranking loss: for query $q_i$, push the score of its relevant passage, the positive, above a **hard negative**, a passage that looks relevant but is not marked relevant (for example one BM25 ranks high), and above the other queries' positives in the same batch (**in-batch negatives**).

blocks.tex: \mathcal{L}_{rank} = -\log \frac{e^{s(q_i, d_i^+)}}{e^{s(q_i, d_i^+)} + e^{s(q_i, d_i^-)} + \sum_j e^{s(q_i, d_{i,j}^-)}}
blocks.caption: In words: a softmax over the scores of the positive, the hard negative and the in-batch negatives gives the positive a probability, and the loss is minus its log. It is near 0 when the positive scores far above all the others and grows as any negative catches up.

blocks.md: The ranking loss alone has no reason to keep vectors sparse: more expansion usually helps recall. So SPLADE adds a sparsity penalty, separately for queries and documents, with two strengths $\lambda_q$ and $\lambda_d$ (more pressure on queries, since query sparsity drives latency):

blocks.caption: Total loss: the ranking loss plus $\lambda_q$ times the FLOPs penalty on queries plus $\lambda_d$ times it on documents. The penalty sums the squares of $\bar a_j$, the average weight of term j over a batch of N texts, a smooth stand-in for the probability that term j is active.

blocks.md: Where does this come from? Paria et al. (ICLR 2020, the International Conference on Learning Representations) observed that with an inverted index, scoring a query against a document costs one multiplication and one addition for each term that is non-zero on both sides. If $p_j^{\text{q}}$ and $p_j^{\text{d}}$ are the probabilities that term $j$ is non-zero in a random query and in a random document, the expected cost is $\sum_j p_j^{\text{q}} p_j^{\text{d}}$: a term costs work only when it is active on both sides. When queries and documents are encoded the same way, both probabilities are the same $p_j$ and the cost becomes $\sum_j p_j^2$. Counting non-zeros is not differentiable, so they replace $p_j$ by the mean absolute weight $\bar a_j$ over a batch, which is why the penalty squares $\bar a_j$. SPLADE reports this same quantity, measured on real vectors, as **FLOPs** in its tables: 0.13 for BM25 and 0.73 for SPLADE on MS MARCO.

The key is the gradient: how fast the penalty grows when one weight grows. Take the weight of term $j$ in document $d_i$. It enters $\bar a_j$ with factor 1/N, and the derivative of $\bar a_j^2$ is $2 \bar a_j$, so the chain rule gives $2 \bar a_j / N$. The usual alternative, the L1 penalty, adds up the absolute values of all weights, so each weight's derivative is just 1/N. Gradient descent subtracts lambda times this push from the weight, moving it toward zero. For one weight of document $d_i$:

blocks.caption: $\ell_1$ as implemented in naver/splade: sum over the vocabulary, mean over the batch. FLOPs pushes harder on terms that carry a lot of weight across the batch.

blocks.title: Push per weight in our 4-document batch (lambda = 1)

scenes.caption: Treat D1 to D4 as one batch. The mean weight of price is 0.74 because it is active in three documents; my is active only in D1 with 0.47, so its mean is 0.117.
FLOPs pushes on price 6 times harder than on my (0.37 versus 0.059). Terms with long, heavy posting lists are the expensive ones, and they get the strongest push.
L1 pushes every active weight equally (0.25), so it cannot tell a cheap rare term from an expensive common one.

blocks.md: To watch the regularizer act, we run projected gradient descent on the batch: ordinary gradient steps, each followed by projecting the weights back into the allowed range, here non-negative. Simplified: a real model gets its pull toward useful weights from the ranking loss through the encoder; here a quadratic pull toward the unregularized weights stands in for it, and weights are clipped at 0 like the ReLU does.

blocks.title: D1's weights as lambda grows (simplified training)

scenes.caption: lambda = 0: the unregularized weights from lesson 2. 8 non-zeros in D1, 18 postings in the batch.
lambda = 1: price in D1 (0.26) hits exactly 0: price is the term with the longest posting list (3 documents). my (0.47) survives at 0.42 because almost nothing else uses it.
lambda = 2: Everything shrinks, frequent terms faster. car, used by D1 and D2, drops from 1.44 to 0.88.
lambda = 4: price is now gone from D4 too, so its posting list has gone from 3 entries to 1. Batch total: 16 postings.
lambda = 8: Weights keep shrinking toward 0; repair falls to 0.11 because D4 also uses it heavily. Too much lambda erases useful signal.

blocks.md: Compare at equal size. FLOPs with lambda = 4 and L1 with lambda = 2 both leave 16 postings. FLOPs removed the two weakest *price* postings (D1 and D4), shrinking the longest list from 3 to 1; L1 removed *my* and *price* from D1. The expected cost $\sum_j p_j^2$ over this batch, with $p_j$ the fraction of the 4 documents in which term $j$ is non-zero, is 1.75 for FLOPs versus 1.875 for L1: the per-term document counts, squared and added, give 28 versus 30, divided by 16, which is 4 documents squared. Same number of non-zeros, cheaper index. The SPLADE paper reports the same pattern at scale: at equal FLOPs, the L1 models were always less effective.

blocks.title: Ramping lambda in during training

scenes.caption: SPLADE follows Paria et al.: lambda grows quadratically until step T (50k in the papers), then stays constant. Early on the encoder learns to rank before it is forced to be sparse.
A short ramp applies full pressure almost immediately, when the weights are still close to the MLM's dense-ish output.

blocks.md: SPLADE is better thought of as a family than one model. The same architecture trained with different lambda values gives anything from very sparse to heavily expanded vectors. The SPLADE paper reports typical lambda values between 0.1 and 0.0001, and a very sparse model with about 18 non-zeros per document and 6 per query still reaching MRR@10 0.296 on MS MARCO.

blocks.question: Two terms have the same weight 0.3 in a document. Term A appears in 1 document of the batch, term B in all of them with similar weights. Under FLOPs, which weight is pushed toward zero faster?
options: A, because rare terms are noise
Both equally, since the weights are equal
B, because its mean weight across the batch is larger, so its gradient 2 a_j / N is larger
Neither; FLOPs only acts on queries
blocks.explain: The FLOPs gradient for a weight is proportional to the term's batch mean. B is active everywhere, so its posting list is long and its push is strong. L1 would treat A and B the same.

blocks.question: After raising lambda_q a lot, MS MARCO MRR@10 drops slightly but queries are much faster. What most likely changed?
options: Document vectors got denser
The vocabulary shrank
The ranking loss switched to L1
Query vectors have fewer non-zeros, so fewer posting lists are traversed
blocks.explain: lambda_q only penalizes the query representation. Fewer query terms means fewer posting lists to read, at some cost in matching power.

lessons.title: Distillation training: MarginMSE, KL and hard negatives worked through

blocks.md: The ranking loss of lesson 4 learns from MS MARCO's labels, which say one thing per query: this passage is relevant, every other passage counts as a negative. That throws away a lot. Some negatives are almost as good as the positive, some are relevant passages nobody labeled, and some are junk. **Distillation** replaces the binary label with graded scores from a slower, more accurate model, the **teacher**. For SPLADE the teacher is a cross-encoder (the *Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together* course, not a prerequisite, builds one), which reads query and passage together. Its scores are computed once, offline, for every training pair, and the SPLADE model, the **student**, is trained to reproduce the teacher's preferences.

Back to the toy. The student scores from lesson 3 for *auto repair* are D1 6.60, D4 4.41, D2 2.69, D3 0. Suppose a cross-encoder teacher gives D4 8.0, D1 7.0, D2 1.0 and D3 -6.0 (illustrative numbers; a cross-encoder outputs an unbounded logit). A binary label might mark only D1. The teacher says more: D4, the one passage about repair, is slightly better than D1, both are far above D2, and D3 is hopeless.

blocks.title: Teacher and student scores for auto repair

scenes.caption: Student (SPLADE, lesson 3): D1 6.60, D4 4.41, D2 2.69, D3 0. It ranks D1 first and leaves D2 only 1.72 below D4.
Teacher (cross-encoder, illustrative): D4 8.0, D1 7.0, D2 1.0, D3 shown as 0 (its score is -6.0). The gaps are what the student should learn: D4 just above D1, D2 far below both.

blocks.caption: Averaged over the training triples. s is the student's score, t the teacher's. Only the margins are compared, so the student keeps its own score scale: the dot products of SPLADE and the logits of a cross-encoder never need to match.

blocks.md:
**MarginMSE** (Hofstatter et al., 2020) trains on triples (query, positive, negative). Compute it for two triples:

- (q, D1, D2): student margin 6.60 - 2.69 = 3.91, teacher margin 7 - 1 = 6, loss $(3.91 - 6)^2 = 4.37$.
- (q, D4, D2): student margin 4.414 - 2.689 = 1.725 (unrounded scores), teacher margin 8 - 1 = 7, loss $(1.725 - 7)^2 = 27.83$.

The batch loss is the mean, 16.10. The second triple dominates: the student badly underrates how much better D4 is than D2. The derivative of the loss with respect to the student's margin is $2(1.725 - 7) = -10.55$; negative means a larger margin lowers the loss.

blocks.tex: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w^{d^+}_j} = 2(\Delta s - \Delta t)\, w^q_j, \qquad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w^{q}_j} = 2(\Delta s - \Delta t)\,\bigl(w^{d^+}_j - w^{d^-}_j\bigr)
blocks.caption: Chain rule through $s(q,d) = \sum_j w^q_j w^d_j$. $\Delta s$ and $\Delta t$ are the student and teacher margins. For the negative document the sign flips.

blocks.title: Gradient on the query weights from the triple (q, D4, D2)

scenes.caption: Each query weight multiplies the difference between D4's and D2's weight on that term. car and auto favor D2 (negative difference); engine, motor, fix and repair favor D4.
Multiply by 2(1.725 - 7) = -10.55: car gets +20.05 and auto +8.44, repair -21.10 and engine -16.88.

Gradient descent moves against the gradient: the query's weights on car and auto go down, those on repair and engine go up. The student learns that, for this query, car is what lets the used car ad score.

blocks.md: Simplified: in the real model the weights are outputs of the encoder, so the gradient flows on into the transformer's parameters, and every weight in the batch moves a little. A weight that is exactly 0 because its logit is negative gets no gradient at all through the ReLU, so distillation reshapes the active terms; the FLOPs terms of lesson 4 decide how many stay active.

blocks.prompt: Use lesson 4's contrastive loss instead, with D1 as the one labeled positive and D2, D3, D4 as negatives. What does that loss do to D4's score, and how does that compare with what the teacher wants?
blocks.reveal: It pushes D4 **down**. The softmax over student scores gives D1 a probability of 0.882, so the loss is already small ($-\log 0.882 = 0.126$), and the only way to lower it further is to raise D1 and lower every other document, D4 included. The teacher wants the opposite: D4 slightly above D1. A binary label cannot express that two passages are both good.

blocks.md: **KL divergence** distills a whole candidate list at once instead of pairs. Turn the teacher's and the student's scores for the same candidates into probability distributions with a softmax, then measure how far the student's distribution is from the teacher's. On the 4 toy documents (D1, D2, D3, D4), the teacher gives 0.269, 0.001, 0.000, 0.731 and the student 0.882, 0.018, 0.001, 0.099, so $\mathrm{KL} = 1.137$. The gradient with respect to each student score is simply student probability minus teacher probability: +0.613 for D1 (push down) and -0.631 for D4 (push up). The *Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one* course (not a prerequisite) covers the temperature that is often applied before the softmax.

blocks.tex: \mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}} = \sum_{i} p^{t}_i \log \frac{p^{t}_i}{p^{s}_i}, \qquad p^{t} = \operatorname{softmax}(t(q, d_1), \dots, t(q, d_n)), \quad p^{s} = \operatorname{softmax}(s(q, d_1), \dots, s(q, d_n))
blocks.caption: In words: for one query and n candidates, the teacher's softmax weights the log ratio of the two distributions. It is 0 only when the student puts the same probabilities on the candidates as the teacher.

blocks.md: Which one does SPLADE use? SPLADE v2 and SPLADE++ trained with MarginMSE. The SPLADE efficiency study (Lassance and Clinchant, 2022) switched to KL because it was more stable in their runs. SPLADE-v3 (2024) uses both, weighted $\lambda_{KL} = 1$ and $\lambda_{MSE} = 0.05$ after cross-validation; its authors observed that with many negatives per query MarginMSE favored recall and KL favored precision. Its teacher scores come from an ensemble of five cross-encoders, normalized per query.

**Where the negatives come from.** BM25 negatives are easy: most are obviously off topic. SPLADE++ (2022) **self-mines**: train a SPLADE model and a cross-encoder, retrieve with that SPLADE model, take its top-ranked non-positive passages as negatives, score them with the cross-encoder and train again. Its **ensemble mining** instead uses a public dataset of MS MARCO negatives, the top 50 from BM25 and from 12 dense retrievers, with cross-encoder scores. SPLADE-v3 mines 100 negatives per query from SPLADE++ (50 from its top 50, 50 at random from its top 1,000) and samples 8 of them per query during training.

Harder negatives include more **false negatives**: relevant passages nobody labeled, which is common when a query has one judged positive. A contrastive loss pushes them down. With a teacher, a false negative gets a score close to the positive's, so its target margin is near 0 and the student is not pushed apart. The SPLADE++ paper notes that distillation is why it needs no extra denoising step.

blocks.caption: The full objective in the SPLADE-v3 style: distillation decides the order, the FLOPs terms from lesson 4 decide how sparse the vectors are. SPLADE v2 and SPLADE++ use the MarginMSE term alone.

blocks.code:
from datasets import Dataset
from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder
from sentence_transformers.sparse_encoder import (
    SparseEncoder, SparseEncoderTrainer, SparseEncoderTrainingArguments)
from sentence_transformers.sparse_encoder.losses import SpladeLoss, SparseMarginMSELoss

student = SparseEncoder("naver/splade-v3-distilbert")
teacher = CrossEncoder("cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2")

# triples (query, positive, hard negative), negatives mined with a first-stage retriever
q, pos, neg = load_triples()
margin = teacher.predict(list(zip(q, pos))) - teacher.predict(list(zip(q, neg)))
train = Dataset.from_dict({"query": q, "positive": pos, "negative": neg,
                           "label": margin.tolist()})

loss = SpladeLoss(student, SparseMarginMSELoss(student),
                  query_regularizer_weight=5e-5,      # lambda_q
                  document_regularizer_weight=3e-5)   # lambda_d
args = SparseEncoderTrainingArguments(output_dir="splade-ft", learning_rate=2e-5,
                                      per_device_train_batch_size=16, num_train_epochs=1)
SparseEncoderTrainer(model=student, args=args, train_dataset=train, loss=loss).train()
blocks.caption: MarginMSE distillation; SpladeLoss adds the FLOPs terms (example weights), ramped up from 0 as in lesson 4. Our smoke run: batch size 8, so 2 steps, on 16 SciFact train claims with BM25 negatives. In 4 of the first 8 this MS MARCO teacher preferred the negative: check the teacher first.

blocks.question: For a triple (q, P, N) the teacher's margin is 4 and the student's is 1. Term j has query weight 0.5, weight 0.8 in P and 0 in N. Which way does one gradient descent step move P's weight on j?
options: Down, because the student's margin is positive already
It does not move, because N has no weight on j
Up: the loss gradient is 2(1 - 4) x 0.5 = -3, so the step raises the weight and the margin
Down, because the FLOPs term always wins over the ranking loss
blocks.explain: The derivative of the loss with respect to P's weight on j is 2(student margin - teacher margin) times the query weight, which is negative here, so descent increases the weight. N's weight on j being 0 only means N's side gets no update on this term.

blocks.question: You mine negatives with your own SPLADE model, and many of the mined 'negatives' are in fact relevant but unlabeled. Which training setup is hurt least?
options: Contrastive loss on the binary labels, because more negatives always help
MarginMSE or KL with cross-encoder scores, because a relevant 'negative' gets a teacher score near the positive's
Any loss, as long as lambda_d is raised
Contrastive loss with BM25 negatives only
blocks.explain: With teacher scores the target for a false negative is a margin near 0 (or a probability near the positive's), so the student is not taught to push it away. A binary contrastive loss treats it as wrong. Raising lambda_d changes sparsity, not the labels.

lessons.title: Why SPLADE queries are slow, and how to make them fast

blocks.md: Lesson 3 ended with a promise: engines skip documents with dynamic pruning. **MaxScore** and **WAND** keep, for each query term, an upper bound on what it can add to any document, and skip a document when the bounds of the terms it could still match cannot lift it above the current k-th best score, the **threshold**. The *Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works* course builds both and **block-max WAND**, which keeps a bound per block of postings. On BM25 they skip most of the work. On SPLADE they mostly do not, and this lesson is about why and what replaces them.

Mackenzie, Trotman and Lin measured this in *Wacky Weights* (2021) on MS MARCO's 8.8 million passages. Two numbers explain most of it. A BM25 query had 5.8 unique terms; a SPLADE v2 query had 25.0, because the query encoder expands too, and many of its tokens are frequent subwords with long posting lists. Documents had 30 unique terms under BM25 and 229 under SPLADE v2. The weights were also odd: for *androgen receptor define*, SPLADE v2 put weight 68 (on its integer impact scale) on a comma and gave stopwords such as *is* and *the* weights of 70 and 56.

blocks.title: MS MARCO query latency, single thread, k = 1000 (Wacky Weights)

scenes.caption: PISA, an efficiency-focused C++ engine running MaxScore: BM25 8.3 ms, SPLADE v2 220.3 ms, about 25 times slower for MRR@10 0.369 instead of 0.187. Encoding time is not included. DeepImpact and uniCOIL-T5 are other learned sparse models (lesson 7).

WAND and block-max WAND did worse than no pruning at all on SPLADE v2: 619 and 681 ms against 553 ms for an exhaustive disjunction. They work to find what to skip, and almost nothing can be. Lucene: 40.1 ms for BM25, 2,140 ms for SPLADE v2.

blocks.md: Why does skipping fail? MaxScore sorts the query terms by bound and calls a prefix **non-essential** while those bounds add up to no more than the threshold: a document that matches only non-essential terms cannot win, so only the essential terms' lists produce candidates. With 2 BM25 terms whose bounds differ a lot, the weaker one quickly becomes non-essential. With dozens of expansion terms, each with a modest bound, the bounds add up past the threshold after only a few terms, so most lists stay essential and almost every document they contain is scored. Flat weight distributions make it worse: many documents score close to each term's maximum, so many come close to the threshold and few can be ruled out.

blocks.prompt: We ran MaxScore (k = 10, our own Python implementation) on SciFact's 5,183 abstracts for the 300 test claims, once with BM25 and once with SPLADE-v3-DistilBERT vectors. How many documents per query do you expect it to score in each case?
blocks.reveal: BM25: each claim has 9.0 terms after stemming and stopword removal, 2,707 abstracts match at least one, and MaxScore scored **852** of them (mean per claim). SPLADE-v3-DistilBERT: claims expand to 124.4 tokens, 5,170 of the 5,183 abstracts match one, and MaxScore still scored **5,006**, 97 percent of the collection. Same algorithm, same exact top 10, almost no skipping. Counts, not times: our Python implementation is only a work meter.

blocks.title: SciFact test claims, per query (k = 10, one run)

scenes.caption: Query terms per claim: BM25 9.0, SPLADE-v3-DistilBERT 124.4, SPLADE++ EnsembleDistil 80.4, and the doc-only model 19.6 (its query is just the claim's tokens).
Postings in those terms' lists, in thousands: 4.2, 101.4, 59.8 and 9.3. Expanded queries pull in frequent subword lists, so a claim touches 14 to 24 times BM25's postings.
Documents MaxScore had to score, out of 5,183: 852, 5,006, 4,782 and 3,224. Even the doc-only queries, 19.6 tokens against 9.0 BM25 terms, skip little here: expanded documents make the lists long.

blocks.md: **Fixes in the model.** Lassance and Clinchant's *Efficiency Study for SPLADE Models* (2022) targeted query length, because on a single CPU thread it is the bottleneck. They trained **separate query and document encoders** (one shared encoder could not be made to produce short queries), replaced the query-side FLOPs penalty with **L1** (which charges every active query weight, matching latency better than FLOPs, which charges a term by how often it is active across the batch), **middle-trained** the language model with an MLM loss plus a FLOPs penalty before fine-tuning, and finally used **BERT-tiny** (a 2-layer BERT with 128-dimensional hidden states) as the query encoder: 0.7 ms per query on their CPU against 45.3 ms for DistilBERT (a 6-layer BERT made smaller by distillation).

blocks.title: Single-thread latency and quality (Lassance and Clinchant 2022)

scenes.caption: Total latency in ms on one CPU core (PISA plus query encoding), on the paper's machine: BM25 4, SPLADE v2 distil 691, BT-SPLADE-S/M/L 7, 13 and 32. BT means a BERT-tiny query encoder.
MS MARCO MRR@10 x 100: 19.7, 36.8, 35.8, 37.6, 38.0. The smallest is within 3 percent of SPLADE v2 at 7 ms, close to BM25's latency (BM25 here drops query stopwords).

But out of domain, on BEIR's 18 datasets (a zero-shot benchmark, lesson 7), mean nDCG@10 x 100: 43.0, 47.0, 39.2, 42.1, 44.5. The fast models lose to BM25 or barely beat it (Quora fell from 0.84 to 0.46). Fusing them with BM25 recovered 45.9 to 48.0.

blocks.md: The extreme of this direction is the **inference-free** or doc-only model from lesson 3: no query encoder, a few query tokens with fixed weights, so the query is as short as a BM25 query. Lesson 7 covers its current form and the lab in lesson 8 measures it.

**Fixes in the index.** The other direction keeps the model and changes traversal. **Score-at-a-time** (SaaT) evaluation stores each posting list sorted by impact instead of document ID and processes postings from the highest impacts down, adding into accumulators, so it can stop after a budget of postings (the JASS engine calls it $\rho$). It barely relies on skipping, so wacky weights hurt it less, and its tail latency is far more predictable. Wacky Weights found it competitive again; its cost is approximation. With a budget of 1 million postings JASS answered SPLADE v2 queries in 15.3 ms, but MRR@10 fell from 0.369 to 0.324; the paper's abstract puts the useful operating points at up to 3 percent effectiveness loss.

**Block-Max Pruning** (BMP; Mallia, Suel and Tonellotto, SIGIR 2024) bounds documents, not terms. Reorder document IDs so similar documents are neighbors (they use a graph-partitioning order called BP), cut the ID range into blocks of $b$ consecutive documents (as few as 8 or 16 documents), and store for every term the maximum weight it has in each block. A query's bound for a block is the sum of query weight times block maximum over its terms. Sort blocks by bound, score whole blocks exactly in that order, and stop when the k-th best score reaches the next block's bound. Stopping there is safe; stopping when the threshold reaches a fraction $\alpha$ of it is approximate. To see it work, extend the toy to 12 documents in 3 blocks:

- B0 (repair): D1, D4, D5 *brake repair shop*, D6 *motor oil change*
- B1 (buying): D2, D7 *car loan rates*, D8 *cheap used auto deals*, D9 *car insurance price*
- B2 (baking): D3, D10 *banana muffin recipe*, D11 *sourdough bread starter*, D12 *fix a soggy bread crust*

Their vectors on the query's terms (illustrative, other terms omitted): D5 repair 1.80, fix 1.10, car 0.90, auto 0.60; D6 motor 1.70, engine 1.20, car 0.80, fix 0.40; D7 car 1.50, auto 0.50; D8 auto 1.70, car 1.20; D9 car 1.30, auto 0.40; D12 fix 1.00, repair 0.20; D10 and D11 have none. D1 to D4 are as before, and the query is still car 0.83, auto 1.39, engine 0.47, motor 0.34, fix 0.96, repair 1.28.

blocks.title: Block-Max Pruning on 12 toy documents, k = 2

scenes.caption: Offline: per block, each term's maximum weight. B0 takes car 1.44 and fix 1.39 from D1, engine 1.60 and repair 2.00 from D4, motor 1.70 from D6. B1 has only car (1.90, D2) and auto (1.70, D8). B2 has only fix 1.00 and repair 0.20 (D12).

Block bounds: B1 = 0.83 x 1.90 + 1.39 x 1.70 = 3.94; B0 = 7.95; B2 = 0.96 x 1.00 + 1.28 x 0.20 = 1.22. B0's bound is loose (the best real score is 6.60) because its maxima come from different documents.
Visit B0 first. The heap is empty, so theta is 0 and the block is scored exactly: D1 6.60, D5 4.94, D4 4.41, D6 2.19. The heap keeps the best 2.
Next is B1 with bound 3.94. theta is now 4.94, the second-best score so far: no document in B1, or in B2 behind it, can reach the top 2. Stop.

Result D1 6.60, D5 4.94, identical to exhaustive scoring. Only 4 of the 12 documents were scored, although 9 of them match some query term; the 5 matching documents in B1 and B2 (best of them D8, 3.36) were ruled out by two block sums.

blocks.md: Block bounds work where term bounds fail because they are computed per region of similar documents: a long query sums many terms, but in a block about baking most of those terms have block maximum 0. On MS MARCO with the SPLADE++ CoCondenser-EnsembleDistil model (lesson 7), k = 10 and exact results, BMP took 10.5 ms per query (b = 32) against 120.6 ms for MaxScore and 614.2 ms for block-max WAND on the same machine. Approximate BMP (b = 64, $\alpha = 0.85$) took 8.1 ms at MRR@10 38.05, against 38.11 for exhaustive search.

**Seismic** (Bruch, Nardini, Rulli and Venturini, SIGIR 2024) goes further into approximation. It rests on what its authors call concentration of importance: for SPLADE on MS MARCO, a query's top 10 weights hold 75 percent of its total weight, and a document's top 50 (about 30 percent of its non-zeros) do the same. So it keeps only each posting list's highest-weight entries, clusters each list into blocks of similar documents (not consecutive IDs), gives each block a summary vector (the per-term maximum over the block, pruned and quantized to one byte), and at query time uses only the query's largest entries, skipping blocks whose summary score is too low compared with the threshold. It reports sub-millisecond single-thread latency on MS MARCO SPLADE vectors at high recall, but results are approximate by design. OpenSearch 3.3 ships it as [neural sparse ANN search](https://docs.opensearch.org/latest/vector-search/ai-search/neural-sparse-ann/) on `sparse_vector` fields.

Two different problems, two kinds of fix. Long, flat queries: shorten them in the model (L1 on queries, a separate small query encoder, query token pruning, or no query encoder at all). Posting lists that defeat per-term bounds: change the index (block maxima over reordered document ranges in BMP, clustered blocks with summaries in Seismic, impact-ordered score-at-a-time traversal).

blocks.question: Which change attacks the query-length problem, and which attacks the posting-list problem?
options: Both are attacked by raising k1 in BM25
Query length: BMP; posting lists: a BERT-tiny query encoder
Query length: L1 regularization on a separate query encoder; posting lists: Block-Max Pruning over reordered document blocks
Both are attacked only by block-max WAND
blocks.explain: L1 on queries and smaller or absent query encoders shrink how many terms a query has. BMP keeps the query as is and changes how documents are grouped and bounded. Block-max WAND is exactly what Wacky Weights found to be slower than no pruning on SPLADE v2.

blocks.question: In the BMP trace, suppose B1 also held a document with car 1.90 and auto 1.70 together. Its bound stays 3.94. Is stopping after B0 still safe?
options: Yes: that document would score 0.83 x 1.90 + 1.39 x 1.70 = 3.94, which cannot beat theta 4.94
No: the bound must be recomputed after every document
No: BMP is always approximate
Yes, but only because B2 is smaller
blocks.explain: A block's bound is at least the score of every document in it, here exactly 3.94 for that document. Since theta is 4.94, no document in B1 can enter the top 2, and B2's bound is lower still. Safety comes from the bound, not from what the block happens to contain.

lessons.title: SPLADE v2, SPLADE++ and running it in production

blocks.md: The architecture has barely changed since 2021; most later gains came from training. SPLADE v2 (2021) introduced max pooling, the doc-only variant and distillation from a cross-encoder teacher with MarginMSE (lesson 5), with negatives mined by a first SPLADE model, which are harder than BM25's. SPLADE++ (SIGIR 2022) added ensembles of mined negatives (hard negatives collected from several different retrievers) and initialization from a retrieval-pretrained CoCondenser checkpoint: CoCondenser (Gao and Callan, 2022) is BERT further pre-trained on the passage collection so that its outputs already suit retrieval.

blocks.title: MS MARCO dev MRR@10 (first-stage retrieval, from the papers)

scenes.caption: Reported MRR@10 x 100. Lexical baselines first: BM25 18.4 and doc2query-T5 27.7 (expansion by generated queries; T5 is the text-to-text transformer that generates them).
Max pooling alone: 32.2 to 34.0. Distillation with mined negatives: 36.8. SPLADE++ with CoCondenser init and ensemble negatives: 38.0, in the range of strong dense retrievers.

blocks.md: **SPLADE-v3 (2024)** is the current Naver baseline. It starts from a SPLADE++ checkpoint and is trained with the mixed KL and MarginMSE loss of lesson 5, teacher scores from an ensemble of cross-encoders and 8 mined negatives per query. Its report gives MRR@10 40.2 on MS MARCO dev and a mean nDCG@10 of 51.7 on 13 datasets of BEIR (the zero-shot benchmark described below), against 37.6 and 50.7 for SPLADE++ SelfDistil, the SPLADE++ variant it started from (the 38.0 in the chart above is EnsembleDistil). Naver released variants on the same recipe: SPLADE-v3-DistilBERT (a smaller encoder), SPLADE-v3-Lexical (no query expansion, so fewer query terms) and SPLADE-v3-Doc (no query encoder at all).

blocks.title: SPLADE-v3 family: in domain versus zero shot (v3 report)

scenes.caption: MS MARCO dev MRR@10 x 100: 40.2, 38.7, 40.0, 37.8. Dropping query expansion (Lexical) costs almost nothing in domain.
Mean BEIR nDCG@10 x 100 over 13 datasets: 51.7, 50.0, 49.1, 47.0. Out of domain, query-side computation matters: no query encoder loses 4.7 points.

blocks.md: The most cited strength is zero-shot transfer: a model trained only on MS MARCO is used on new datasets with no further training. BEIR (Thakur et al. 2021) is a benchmark of 18 retrieval datasets from different domains, such as biomedical search, fact checking and argument retrieval, built to test exactly this. The SPLADE v2 paper evaluates the readily available BEIR datasets with NDCG@10 (a ranking metric that rewards relevant documents near the top of the first 10 results). Each relevant result in the top 10 adds its relevance divided by log2 of its rank plus 1, so rank 1 counts fully and rank 3 counts half, and the sum is divided by the same sum for the ideal ranking so a perfect order scores exactly 1.

Averaged over its 14 datasets (13 zero-shot ones plus MS MARCO), DistilSPLADE-max (the distilled SPLADE v2 with max pooling) scored 0.500 against BM25 0.440, ColBERT 0.455 and the dense TAS-B 0.435, a dense retriever trained with topic-aware sampling and distillation. On the 13 zero-shot datasets alone it scored 0.506, and SPLADE++ later reported 50.5 and 50.7 (x 100) on that 13-dataset subset. Two of those datasets show why averages are not enough. TREC-COVID comes from TREC, the Text REtrieval Conference run by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology: COVID-19 questions searched over scientific papers. Touche-2020 asks for arguments on controversial questions, searched over debate websites.

blocks.title: BEIR NDCG@10: averages hide failures

scenes.caption: Average over the 14 datasets of SPLADE v2's BEIR table (13 zero-shot plus MS MARCO): the distilled SPLADE leads.
TREC-COVID (biomedical): SPLADE 0.710 is best, the dense model drops to 0.481.
Touche-2020 (argument retrieval): plain BM25 at 0.614 beats every neural model; SPLADE gets 0.364. Always evaluate on your own data.

blocks.md: **Inference-free models today.** SPLADE-doc gave every query token weight 1. Current inference-free models learn or fix a weight per vocabulary token instead. OpenSearch's v3 doc models load a query side that is a tokenizer plus a weight lookup table shipped with the model (an IDF table, idf.json), so a rare token counts more than a common one, as in BM25. Geng et al. (2024) also put IDF into training, scoring $\sum_t \mathrm{idf}(t)\, q_t\, d_t$, so the ranking gradient on a document token grows with its IDF while the FLOPs penalty does not: frequent, uninformative tokens get pruned and informative ones survive. They report 3.3 points of mean BEIR nDCG@10 over the previous best inference-free model; OpenSearch's doc-v3-distill card reports 0.517 on its 13 BEIR datasets against 0.490 for its first doc model.

**Related learned sparse models.** DeepImpact (Mallia et al., SIGIR 2021) first expands documents with doc2query-T5, then learns one impact score per document term; the query is an unweighted bag of words and the score is the sum of impacts of matching terms. COIL (contextualized inverted lists, Gao, Dai and Callan, 2021) stores a small contextual vector for each document token in its posting list and scores exact token matches by vector dot products. uniCOIL (Lin and Ma, 2021) shrinks those per-token vectors to a single ReLU weight, again with doc2query-T5 expansion, and runs on a standard Lucene index (1.3 GB for MS MARCO in their notes). SPLADE differs by learning expansion and weighting jointly in one model, on both query and document side.

blocks.title: A learned sparse pipeline in a search engine

scenes.caption: Indexing: every chunk goes through the transformer once and is stored as token-weight pairs. Elastic stores the output of its model ELSER (Elastic Learned Sparse Encoder) in a sparse_vector field; OpenSearch in rank_features, or sparse_vector for ANN (3.3+).
Bi-encoder mode: the query also runs through the encoder, gets expanded, and is scored against the posting lists. Best relevance, but a transformer call per query and more terms to traverse.
Doc-only mode: the query encoder becomes a tokenizer plus fixed per-token weights. OpenSearch's default; faster, slightly less relevant.

Query pruning: drop low-weight query tokens, or score with high-weight tokens first and rescore the top documents with the rest (OpenSearch two-phase processor). The result can then be reranked or fused with a dense retriever.

blocks.md: **What the production docs say.** Elastic's ELSER is a learned sparse model trained by Elastic for English; its docs say it encodes only the first 512 tokens of a field (chunk longer text), that ELSER v2 used an improved FLOPs regularizer, and that by default Elasticsearch prunes query tokens that are both very frequent (more than 5 times the average token frequency) and low weight (below 0.4). OpenSearch added neural sparse search in 2.11, stores token-weight pairs in a rank features index, and recommends doc-only mode as the default trade-off.

Do not read the tokens as an explanation. Elastic's docs warn that expansion terms are learned associations, not synonyms, and that low-weight tokens carry information jointly, much like dimensions of a dense vector. A surprising token in a result is not by itself a bug.

**Trade-offs to remember.**

- Index and latency grow with expansion; lambda, query pruning, a small or absent query encoder, and SPLADE-aware traversal such as BMP (lesson 6) are the knobs.
- Indexing needs a transformer pass per chunk; BM25 needs none.
- The vocabulary is the model's WordPiece vocabulary, mostly English for BERT-based models. Rare identifiers split into subwords, so exact-code matching can still favor BM25, which is why hybrids with BM25 often add gains (SPLADE++ reports this on BEIR).
- Models are trained on MS MARCO passages; long documents must be chunked.

blocks.question: Your corpus is 3,000-token technical manuals. You index each manual whole with ELSER and recall is poor for facts near the end. Most likely cause?
options: ELSER encodes only the first 512 tokens of a field, so later text never reaches the index
The FLOPs regularizer removed rare terms
Doc-only mode ignores the document
BM25 fusion is required for ELSER to work
blocks.explain: Elastic's docs state ELSER uses the first 512 tokens of a field and recommend chunking larger fields into multiple values below that limit.

blocks.question: You need the lowest query latency on CPU-only search nodes but still want expansion. Which setup fits best?
options: Bi-encoder SPLADE with lambda_q = 0
Dense retrieval with HNSW
Doc-only sparse mode: expand documents at index time, tokenize queries with fixed weights
BM25 with doc length normalization disabled
blocks.explain: Doc-only mode keeps expansion on the document side, computed offline, and runs no transformer at query time. lambda_q = 0 would make queries denser and slower.

blocks.question: On a new dataset, SPLADE loses to BM25. Which explanation is consistent with the BEIR numbers above?
options: SPLADE cannot represent exact matches
BM25 always wins on BEIR
The FLOPs regularizer forbids matching rare terms
Learned models can underperform BM25 on some out-of-domain tasks (Touche-2020 is one), so you must evaluate per dataset
blocks.explain: SPLADE keeps exact term matching and wins on average, but on Touche-2020 BM25 scored 0.614 versus 0.364. Averages hide such failures.

lessons.title: Build it: encode, index and evaluate SPLADE on SciFact

blocks.md: Now run real models. The collection is BEIR's **SciFact**, as in the search courses: 5,183 scientific abstracts, and 300 test claims as queries, each with about one relevant abstract. The baselines line up with those courses: BM25 from *BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting* ($k_1 = 1.2$, $b = 0.75$, Porter stemming, `bm25s`' stop list, title and abstract as one field) scores nDCG@10 0.677, and the small dense embedding model all-MiniLM-L6-v2 from *Text embeddings and semantic search* (not a prerequisite) 0.645. Everything below ran on one CPU with two threads; rerun it rather than trusting copied figures.

Three sparse models, all through Sentence Transformers' `SparseEncoder`:

- **naver/splade-v3-distilbert**, the main one. The full naver/splade-v3 is gated on Hugging Face (you must accept its terms), so we use its DistilBERT version, 67M parameters.
- **naver/splade-cocondenser-ensembledistil**, the SPLADE++ model of lesson 7 (BERT-base, 110M), called SPLADE++ ED here.
- **opensearch-neural-sparse-encoding-doc-v3-distill**, inference-free: a DistilBERT document encoder and a query side that is a tokenizer plus a weight table.

We cut inputs at 256 tokens, the setting the Naver model cards give for reproducing their evaluations. That truncates 3,681 of the 5,183 abstracts (they average 337 tokens), a choice to revisit for your own data.

import torch, scipy.sparse as sp
from sentence_transformers import SparseEncoder
torch.set_num_threads(2)

model = SparseEncoder("naver/splade-v3-distilbert", device="cpu")
model.max_seq_length = 256                      # the card's evaluation setting
texts = [d["title"] + " " + d["text"] for d in corpus]          # 5,183 abstracts

def to_csr(t):                                  # torch sparse COO to scipy CSR
    t = t.coalesce(); i = t.indices().numpy()
    return sp.csr_matrix((t.values().numpy(), (i[0], i[1])), shape=tuple(t.shape))

D = to_csr(model.encode_document(texts, batch_size=16, convert_to_sparse_tensor=True))
Q = to_csr(model.encode_query([queries[q] for q in qids], convert_to_sparse_tensor=True))
print(D.shape, D.nnz / D.shape[0], Q.nnz / Q.shape[0])     # vectors are 30,522 wide

q = model.encode_query([queries[qids[0]]])
print(model.decode(q[0], top_k=15))             # (token, weight) pairs, heaviest first
blocks.caption: Step 1: encode documents and test claims into sparse vectors. On our 2-thread CPU, encoding the corpus took 261 s with the DistilBERT model and 555 s with BERT-base SPLADE++; times vary by machine.

blocks.md: Decode one vector before trusting any score. Test claim 1 is *0-dimensional biomaterials show inductive properties.* SPLADE-v3-DistilBERT encodes it into 56 non-zero tokens. The heaviest are pieces of the claim's own words, because WordPiece splits *biomaterials* into bio, ##mate, ##rial and *inductive* into ind, ##uc, ##tive: bio 2.29, 0 2.20, ##mate 2.09, ind 2.06, dimensional 1.97. Then come expansion terms the claim never uses: material 1.54, biological 1.50, zero 1.48, dimension 1.24, property 1.03, shape 0.97.

blocks.prompt: The relevant abstract is titled *New opportunities: the use of nanotechnologies to manipulate and track stem cells*, 91 words that never contain bio, material or biology. Will SPLADE give the pair a positive score, and through which terms?
blocks.reveal: Yes, 5.94, and only through expansion on both sides. The abstract's 268-token vector carries bio, material, biology, type and chemistry although its text has none of them. The largest products are bio 1.25, material 0.98 and biology 0.74. BM25 can match this pair only on words both texts literally share. The doc-only model scores the same pair 0.64, matching on bio alone: its query cannot add material or biology.

import numpy as np

Dq = D.copy()
Dq.data = np.round(Dq.data * 100)               # integer impacts, factor 100
Dq.eliminate_zeros()                            # weights under 0.005 vanish
index = Dq.tocsc()                              # column t = posting list of token t

def search(qrow, k=100):                        # term-at-a-time, as in lesson 3
    acc = np.zeros(index.shape[0])
    for t, w in zip(qrow.indices, qrow.data):
        lo, hi = index.indptr[t], index.indptr[t + 1]
        acc[index.indices[lo:hi]] += w * index.data[lo:hi]
    top = np.argpartition(-acc, k)[:k]
    return top[np.argsort(-acc[top])]

def ndcg10(ranked, rel):                        # rel: {doc id: grade}
    dcg = sum(rel.get(ids[d], 0) / np.log2(i + 2) for i, d in enumerate(ranked[:10]))
    ideal = sorted(rel.values(), reverse=True)[:10]
    return dcg / sum(g / np.log2(i + 2) for i, g in enumerate(ideal))

scores = [ndcg10(search(Q.getrow(i)), qrels[q]) for i, q in enumerate(qids)]
print(np.mean(scores))

blocks.title: SciFact test, 300 claims: nDCG@10 (one run)

scenes.caption: Single retrievers: BM25 0.677, MiniLM 0.645, SPLADE-v3-DistilBERT 0.685 (the v3 report lists 68.5 for this model on SciFact), SPLADE++ ED 0.702, doc-only 0.690.

Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF, k = 60), adding 1/(60 + rank) from the BM25 and MiniLM rankings (*Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval*, not a prerequisite), reaches 0.718. In this run no sparse model alone reached it; that 0.016 gap was not tested.

blocks.md: Are those gains real? Test them per claim, as in *Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG* (not a prerequisite; paired t-test, and a randomization test that flips the sign of each claim's difference). Against BM25 none is significant: SPLADE-v3-DistilBERT +0.008 (60 claims up, 50 down, p = 0.64), SPLADE++ ED +0.025 (63 up, 42 down, p = 0.09, 95 percent bootstrap interval -0.003 to 0.054), doc-only +0.013 (p = 0.37). Against MiniLM all three are: +0.040 (p = 0.014), +0.057 (p = 0.0003) and +0.045 (p = 0.004). Recall@100 (the share of a claim's relevant abstracts found in the top 100) is 0.919, 0.932 and 0.924 against BM25's 0.919. SciFact is a domain where BM25 is strong; the BEIR averages of lesson 7 hide exactly this. For scale, doc2query document expansion moved the same BM25 from 0.677 to 0.687 in *Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites* (not a prerequisite), also not significant.

The doc-only model's card lists SciFact among its training datasets, so its 0.690 is not a zero-shot number. Check a model's training data before calling a benchmark result transfer. Its card reports 0.708 on SciFact; our 256-token run gives 0.690. Quantizing to integer impacts cost nothing here: nDCG@10 moved by at most 0.0013 for each model.

scenes.caption: Postings per abstract: 96 stemmed BM25 terms, 296 for SPLADE-v3-DistilBERT, 190 for SPLADE++ ED, 234 for the doc-only model. Document expansion makes the index two to three times larger.

Uncompressed index in MB, at 4 bytes per document ID plus 2 per impact (at factor 100 SPLADE impacts reach 320 and 338, too large for one byte; the doc-only peak, 140, would fit): 3.0, 9.1, 5.9 and 7.0.

blocks.md:
**Checklist for production.**

1. Chunk documents to the model's limit (512 tokens, 256 in these evaluations); text past it never reaches the index.
2. Quantize weights to integer impacts and check the metric does not move.
3. Decide the query side: bi-encoder for quality, doc-only when query latency or CPU cost rules, and prune low-weight query tokens either way.
4. Use a SPLADE-aware engine or traversal (lesson 6) if latency matters at scale.
5. Evaluate on your own queries against BM25 with paired tests, and consider fusing with BM25, which the *Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval* and *Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)* courses cover (neither is a prerequisite).

blocks.question: You switch from one SPLADE checkpoint to another of the same size and the index doubles, while queries are unchanged. Which training choice most likely differs?
options: A weaker document-side sparsity penalty (smaller lambda_d), so documents keep more expansion terms
A larger query-side lambda_q
Integer quantization with factor 100
Max pooling instead of sum pooling
blocks.explain: Index size is total postings, which lambda_d controls through the document FLOPs term. lambda_q only shapes queries. Quantization and pooling do not double the number of non-zeros. In our run SPLADE-v3-DistilBERT and SPLADE++ ED gave 296 and 190 postings per abstract, though they also differ in size and training.

blocks.question: On SciFact, SPLADE++ ED beat BM25 by 0.025 nDCG@10 with p = 0.09. What should you report?
options: SPLADE++ is significantly better than BM25 on SciFact
BM25 is better, because p is above 0.05
A small gain that this test set cannot distinguish from noise, with its interval (-0.003 to 0.054)
Nothing, since BEIR already shows SPLADE wins on average
blocks.explain: With 300 claims the interval still includes 0, so the gain is plausible but not established. It does not show BM25 is better either. A BEIR average says nothing certain about one dataset.
